The House of Valois. Ruling France from 1328 to 1589, the Valois presided over some of medieval Europe's grandest and bloodiest conflicts—the Hundred Years' War, the Wars of Religion, and the Italian Wars. Though overshadowed by external warfare and internal religious strife, they patronized the arts and learning, helping usher in the French Renaissance before their line was extinguished by the rise of the House of Bourbon.

Philip VI ascended the throne in 1328 after the extinction of the Capetian line, founding the dynasty that would rule France for over two hundred sixty years. They fought the Hundred Years' War from 1337 to 1453 with England over the French succession. This war saw the campaigns of Joan of Arc, who rallied France to military victories. Francis I reigned from 1515 to 1547 and embodied Renaissance kingship. He was a patron of art and learning who commissioned the châteaux of the Loire Valley and rivaled Henry VIII in cultural ambition and martial prowess.

The Valois fought the Italian Wars against the Habsburgs for control of territories in Italy—a prolonged struggle that weakened both powers. Later Valois kings faced the Wars of Religion from 1562 to 1598, brutal civil conflicts between Catholics and Huguenots, French Protestants, that fractured the realm. Catherine de Medici, an Italian queen, wielded enormous power during the minority and weakness of later Valois kings. She orchestrated the Saint Bartholomew's Day Massacre in 1572. The dynasty ended with Henry III, who was assassinated in 1589. The crown passed to Henry IV of Bourbon, uniting the two houses.
